title: Globular Star Cluster M4
caption: The globular cluster Messier 4, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: M 4, Messier 4, NGC 6121 · constellation Scorpius · about 7000 light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Thousands of bright points of light fill this Hubble view, gathered a little more thickly towards the centre. Their colours vary. The most prominent look blue or yellow-orange, and the brighter ones show four diffraction spikes, an effect of the telescope's structure. This is Messier 4, a globular cluster.

A globular cluster is a dense, roughly spherical swarm of stars bound together by gravity, and Messier 4 holds several hundred thousand of them. The colours of the stars carry information, since hotter stars generally look bluer and cooler stars redder.

Messier 4 may also hide something in its core. Astronomers suspect an unseen intermediate-mass black hole of up to 800 solar masses sits there. Such black holes would sit between the small ones left by single stars and the giants at galaxy centres, but whether one really exists here is not yet confirmed.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (3.48 x 3.45 arcminutes) and distance (7000 light years), the frame spans roughly 7.1 × 7 light-years. Its light set out about 7,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys imaged the cluster through blue, visible and near-infrared filters. The source does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and the four-pointed spikes around bright stars come from the telescope, not the stars.

behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: Messier 4 lies about 7000 light-years away. The image was taken with Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys.
alt: Thousands of blue and yellow-orange stars on a black background, more concentrated near the centre, with spikes on the brightest.
